body.heading: The day is full of thresholds
paragraphs: Between activities, we usually carry the last thing straight into the next: the argument into the meeting, the meeting into lunch, the whole day into the evening. The mind gets no moment to close a file before opening another, and by evening everything is open at once.
A one-minute pause is a threshold ritual. Sixty seconds, deliberately empty, placed at the joints of the day. It is too small to schedule around and too useful to skip — the ideal size for a habit.

body.heading: How to spend a minute doing nothing
paragraphs: Stop where you are. Let your eyes rest on something far away or gently closed. Breathe slowly, and let the out-breath be long. Feel your feet, your seat, the air. Let the previous activity finish echoing without reviewing it, and do not preview the next one yet. You are not resting from the day; you are arriving at the next part of it.

A timer helps at first — a minute is longer than it feels when you are busy, and shorter than it feels when you are stressed. Either way, it ends, and you go on, carrying a little less of the last hour with you.

body.heading: Attach pauses to doors that already exist
paragraphs: The pause needs a trigger, and the day provides them: the moment before you open a meeting, the walk back from making tea, the car before the engine starts, the doorstep before you go in. Choose one doorway to begin with and put your minute there, every time.

People who build this habit often say the minute starts to feel like the most honest moment of the hour. Everything else is doing. This is the breath between the sentences — and sentences need their breaths.

takeaway: At the joints of the day, stop for one full minute and arrive before you begin.
